# Loop Closure and Long-Term Consistency {#sec-loop-closure}

Loop closure occurs when a robot recognizes that it has returned to a previously
visited place. The measurement is not just "I see a feature." It is "this
current region corresponds to that old region," and it arrives as a constraint
between the present pose and a pose from minutes or hours ago.

Navigators have done a version of this for centuries. A ship's officer who has
run on dead reckoning all night takes a bearing on a charted lighthouse at dawn
and discovers the ship is two miles from where the plot says. That fix is
absolute, because the lighthouse is on the chart. A robot doing SLAM has no
chart. Its lighthouse is a piece of its own map, built earlier from the same
drifting estimate. Loop closure is the art of using your own old, imperfect map
as the chart, which is why it is powerful and also why it is dangerous.

It matters because dead reckoning drifts. A four-kilometer drive through
Victoria Park can look locally plausible while ending up globally misaligned,
and loop closure is the mechanism that pulls the trajectory back into
consistency. This chapter covers how revisits are recognized and verified, why
filters and smoothers respond so differently to them, and then builds a small
pose-graph optimizer from scratch, breaks it with a false loop closure, and
repairs it with a robust kernel.

In Project 2, loop closure is something to analyze rather than implement: the
project covers feature extraction, association, and FastSLAM, and asks you to
explain what your results say about revisits (see @sec-project2 and
@sec-loop-closure-project-report).

## Why Drift Accumulates {#sec-loop-closure-why-drift-accumulates}

Suppose odometry has a small heading bias. Each short motion update looks
reasonable. A constant heading error $\delta\psi$ produces a cross-track error
that grows linearly with distance, roughly $d\,\delta\psi$ after $d$ meters. A
heading error that random-walks is worse: the position error then grows like
$d^{3/2}$, because every heading error is integrated twice. When the robot
returns near the start, the estimated pose may be far from where the map says
it should be.

This is the essential loop-closure pattern:

1. the robot revisits an old place;
2. the front end proposes a match to prior map structure;
3. the system verifies the match geometrically;
4. the back end uses the constraint to reduce accumulated drift.

The difficult part is that a false loop closure can be worse than no loop
closure. A single confident wrong match can bend the map into nonsense, and
@sec-loop-closure-robust-kernels shows it happening.

## Recognition and Verification {#sec-loop-closure-recognition-verification}

Loop closure has two stages. **Place recognition** finds candidate revisited
locations, and **geometric verification** checks whether a candidate is
physically consistent and measures the relative pose it implies.

Place recognition is a retrieval problem rather than an estimation problem: the
question is "which old place does this look like?", not "what is my pose?". The
cheapest recognizer is the pose estimate itself: search only the old poses that
fall inside the current position uncertainty. That works for short loops and
fails exactly when loop closure matters most, after a long excursion, when the
uncertainty ellipse has grown large enough to contain half the map. Practical
systems therefore recognize places from what the sensor sees, independently of
the estimate, and use the estimate only to rank or sanity-check candidates.

### Appearance-Based Recognition {#sec-loop-closure-appearance-recognition}

Cameras see a great deal of appearance, and the classic way to search it is a
**bag of words**. Local descriptors such as ORB or SIFT (@sec-visual-nav-features-descriptors)
are quantized into a vocabulary of "visual words," learned offline by clustering
descriptors from many images. An image becomes a sparse histogram of word counts,
weighted so that words appearing in every image (asphalt, sky) count for little,
and an inverted index from words to images makes retrieval over thousands of
keyframes take milliseconds. DBoW2 [@galvezlopez2012dbow] does this with binary
descriptors and a hierarchical vocabulary, requires a loop to be confirmed by
several consecutive frames before reporting it, and is the loop detector inside
ORB-SLAM (@sec-visual-nav-orb-slam-as). Learned global descriptors such as
NetVLAD [@arandjelovic2016netvlad] replace the hand-built vocabulary with a
neural network trained so that images of the same place land close together
even across changes of lighting, weather, and season.

### Geometry-Based Recognition {#sec-loop-closure-geometry-recognition}

Lidar scans carry little appearance but a lot of shape. Scan Context
[@kim2018scancontext] bins a 3D scan into a polar grid of rings and sectors
around the sensor and stores the maximum point height in each bin. Two such
descriptors are compared over all circular shifts of the sector axis, which
makes the comparison independent of the vehicle's heading at the two visits.

For a landmark map such as Victoria Park's trees, the natural descriptor is the
constellation itself. Distances between pairs of trees, and the trunk diameters,
do not change under a planar rigid motion, so a local group of trees seen now can
be compared with groups in the old map by matching triangles or sets of
inter-tree distances. This is the same trick a spacecraft star tracker uses for
"lost in space" attitude determination: it matches the angles between observed
stars against triangles in its onboard catalog. Two correctly matched trees are
enough to hypothesize the planar transform between the old and new visits.

### Geometric Verification {#sec-loop-closure-geometric-verification}

A candidate is only a hypothesis. Verification fits a geometric model to the
correspondences the candidate proposes, robustly. RANSAC [@fischler1981ransac]
repeatedly samples a minimal set (two tree pairs for a planar transform, five
points for an essential matrix, three or four for PnP; see
@sec-visual-nav-geometry-checks), keeps the model with the most inliers, and
rejects the candidate if too few correspondences agree. The surviving transform
is then refined by scan matching (iterative closest point [@besl1992icp] or a
correlative matcher on lidar, reprojection-error minimization on images), which
also provides the covariance of the relative pose.

The output of a verified loop closure is therefore a measurement like any other:
a relative pose between two poses, with an information matrix. The rest of this
chapter is about what the back end does with it.

## Why Filtering SLAM Struggles {#sec-loop-closure-why-filtering-slam}

Filtering methods estimate the current state and fold everything else into it.
That does not mean a filter cannot correct the past map. When EKF-SLAM
re-observes an old landmark at the end of a loop, the innovation is large, and
the update moves not only the robot but every landmark correlated with it. The
dense cross-covariances of @sec-slam-ekf-slam-one are precisely the memory that
carries the correction around the whole loop, and for a linear-Gaussian problem
the filter's final map would be identical to the batch solution.

What a filter cannot do is **relinearize** the past. The old poses have been
marginalized out (@sec-information-filter-marginalization-conditioning shows
how that fills in the information matrix; see @fig-information-fill-in), and
every Jacobian along the way was evaluated at the estimate available at that
moment. After a long loop with a large heading error those linearization points
were wrong, and the errors they caused are baked permanently into the mean and
covariance. The filter becomes overconfident, which is the EKF-SLAM
inconsistency analyzed by Huang, Mourikis, and Roumeliotis [@huang2010]. The
iterated EKF (@sec-ekf-iterated-ekf) relinearizes the current update but cannot
reach back to earlier ones. Add the cost of updating a dense covariance that
grows with the square of the map size, and EKF-SLAM struggles on long loops for
reasons of both accuracy and arithmetic.

FastSLAM has a different weakness. Each particle carries a complete path
hypothesis and its own map, so a revisit re-weights the particles: those whose
map agrees with what the robot sees gain weight. That works only if a particle
with a good path is still alive. Resampling repeatedly discards low-weight
paths, and over a long loop the particle set can collapse onto a few ancestors
from the middle of the loop. Then:

- If the correct old trajectory hypothesis survives, FastSLAM benefits from
  revisiting known landmarks.
- If the correct hypothesis was resampled away, the filter cannot recover it
  later.
- If the map contains duplicate landmarks, the system may treat a revisited
  place as new territory.

This is why particle count, process noise, data association, and resampling
threshold all affect long-loop behavior.

## Why GraphSLAM Handles Loops Naturally {#sec-loop-closure-why-graphslam-handles}

GraphSLAM keeps past poses as variables
[@DurrantWhyteBailey2006SLAMTutorial; @dellaert2006]. Odometry, landmark
observations, GPS fixes, and loop closures all become **factors** that each
constrain a few of those variables, and the optimizer adjusts the whole
trajectory to satisfy them together. Because the past poses are still
variables, the optimizer relinearizes them at every iteration; nothing is baked
in.

In a **pose graph** the variables are the poses themselves. Write planar pose
$i$ as a homogeneous matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}_i &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{C}(\theta_i) & \mathbf{t}_i \\
\mathbf{0}^T & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\in SE(2), \\
\mathbf{C}(\theta) &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\
\sin\theta & \cos\theta
\end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\theta_i$ measured counter-clockwise from the world $x$ axis. In the
notation of @sec-frames-camera-transforms, $\mathbf{X}_i$ is
$\mathbf{T}_{b_i}^w$, the pose of the body at time $i$ in the world. The pose of
$j$ as seen from $i$ is $\mathbf{X}_i^{-1}\mathbf{X}_j$, and that is what both
odometry and a loop closure measure: a relative pose $\mathbf{Z}_{ij}$ with
information matrix $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}$. The residual must compare the
predicted and measured relative poses *on the group*:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{ij} = \mathbf{Z}_{ij}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_i^{-1}\mathbf{X}_j,
\qquad
\mathbf{e}_{ij} = \operatorname{Log}\left(\mathbf{E}_{ij}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^3.
$$ {#eq-loop-closure-se2-residual}

If the measurement is satisfied exactly, $\mathbf{E}_{ij}$ is the identity and
$\mathbf{e}_{ij} = \mathbf{0}$. $\operatorname{Log}$ maps a group element to
its tangent vector, the three numbers of translation and rotation "left over"
[@barfoot2017]. The same formula holds in 3D with $\mathbf{X} \in SE(3)$, where
$\operatorname{Log}$ returns six numbers: three of translation and a rotation
vector.

Writing the residual as plain subtraction, $\mathbf{z}_{ij} - (\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i)$,
is tempting and wrong in two ways. The simplest symptom is the angle. A robot
heading $179^\circ$ at pose $i$ and $-179^\circ$ at pose $j$ has turned
$2^\circ$, but subtraction reports $-358^\circ$, and the optimizer will dutifully
try to spin part of the map through a full turn to fix it. Wrapping the heading
difference into $[-\pi, \pi)$ repairs that symptom (@sec-ukf-angles). The deeper
problem is the translation: odometry measures how far the robot moved *in its own
frame at pose $i$*, so the predicted translation is
$\mathbf{C}(\theta_i)^T(\mathbf{t}_j - \mathbf{t}_i)$, not
$\mathbf{t}_j - \mathbf{t}_i$. Subtraction works only for a robot that always
faces along the world $x$ axis. In 3D there is no single angle to wrap, and the traps are quaternion
sign flips and rotation vectors near $\pi$ (@sec-ukf-attitude).

Carrying out the products for $SE(2)$, with $\mathbf{Z}_{ij}$ built from the
measured translation $\mathbf{t}_z$ and rotation $\theta_z$, the error
transform $\mathbf{E}_{ij}$ has rotation angle and translation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{ij} &= \operatorname{wrap}\left(\theta_j - \theta_i - \theta_z\right), \\
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{ij} &= \mathbf{C}(\theta_z)^T
\left[\mathbf{C}(\theta_i)^T\left(\mathbf{t}_j - \mathbf{t}_i\right) - \mathbf{t}_z\right].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-loop-closure-se2-error-parts}

The exact logarithm is
$\operatorname{Log}(\mathbf{E}_{ij}) = [\mathbf{V}(\phi_{ij})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{ij};\ \phi_{ij}]$,
with

$$
\mathbf{V}(\phi) = \frac{1}{\phi}
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin\phi & -(1 - \cos\phi) \\
1 - \cos\phi & \sin\phi
\end{bmatrix}
= \mathbf{I} + O(\phi).
$$

In a converged graph the leftover rotation $\phi_{ij}$ is a fraction of a degree,
so $\mathbf{V} \approx \mathbf{I}$, and most 2D solvers, including g2o's planar
edges and the tutorial of Grisetti et al. [@grisetti2010tutorial], use the
simpler residual $\mathbf{e}_{ij} = [\boldsymbol{\tau}_{ij};\ \phi_{ij}]$. It
vanishes exactly when the logarithm does, differs from it only at second order
in the error, and has short Jacobians. The code below uses it and then checks how
far it is from the exact $\operatorname{Log}$ at the solution.

The optimizer minimizes the sum of squared Mahalanobis norms over all edges
$\mathcal{E}$, odometry and loop closures alike:

$$
\mathbf{X}^\star = \arg\min_{\mathbf{X}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{X}_{n-1}}
\sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathbf{e}_{ij}^T\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\,\mathbf{e}_{ij}.
$$ {#eq-loop-closure-pose-graph-cost}

The mathematical reference (@sec-math-reference-pose-graph-optimization) gives
the general Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt machinery. The next section
builds it for one concrete loop.

## A Pose Graph from Scratch {#sec-loop-closure-pose-graph}

The robot drives 1 m steps around a 10 m square, turning left at each corner,
for one and a quarter laps. Its odometry has white noise and also a small
heading bias of $0.6^\circ$ per step that the noise model knows nothing about,
the slowly accumulating error of @sec-loop-closure-why-drift-accumulates. When
the robot returns to the start at pose 40, the front end recognizes the place
and verifies a loop closure to pose 0. Nothing else is detected on the second
pass; this front end is conservative.

First, the $SE(2)$ helpers. `v2t` and `t2v` convert between the pose vector
$\mathbf{x}_i = [x_i, y_i, \theta_i]^T$ and the matrix $\mathbf{X}_i$;
`relative_pose` computes $\mathbf{X}_i^{-1}\mathbf{X}_j$, which is what an
odometry or loop-closure measurement reports; `se2_log` is the exact logarithm,
used only as a check.

```{python}
#| label: loop-closure-se2-helpers
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
import scipy.sparse.linalg as spla


def wrap_angle(angle):
    """Wrap an angle (or array of angles) to [-pi, pi)."""
    return (angle + np.pi) % (2.0 * np.pi) - np.pi


def rot2(theta):
    """2x2 rotation matrix C(theta), theta counter-clockwise from +x."""
    c, s = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)
    return np.array([[c, -s], [s, c]])


def v2t(pose):
    """Pose vector (x, y, theta) -> 3x3 homogeneous SE(2) matrix X."""
    X = np.eye(3)
    X[:2, :2] = rot2(pose[2])
    X[:2, 2] = pose[:2]
    return X


def t2v(X):
    """3x3 homogeneous SE(2) matrix -> pose vector (x, y, theta)."""
    return np.array([X[0, 2], X[1, 2], np.arctan2(X[1, 0], X[0, 0])])


def relative_pose(pose_i, pose_j):
    """Pose j expressed in the frame of pose i: t2v(X_i^-1 X_j)."""
    return t2v(np.linalg.inv(v2t(pose_i)) @ v2t(pose_j))


def compose(pose, delta):
    """Apply the relative motion `delta` (in the frame of `pose`): t2v(X Delta)."""
    return t2v(v2t(pose) @ v2t(delta))


def se2_log(X):
    """Exact SE(2) logarithm [rho; phi], where the translation is V(phi) rho."""
    phi = np.arctan2(X[1, 0], X[0, 0])
    if abs(phi) < 1e-9:
        return np.array([X[0, 2], X[1, 2], phi])
    a, b = np.sin(phi) / phi, (1.0 - np.cos(phi)) / phi
    V = np.array([[a, -b], [b, a]])
    return np.append(np.linalg.solve(V, X[:2, 2]), phi)
```

Next, the simulated drive. Every edge is a tuple `(i, j, z_ij, Omega_ij)`: a
measurement of pose $j$ relative to pose $i$ and its information matrix. The
initial guess for the optimizer is plain dead reckoning, the odometry chained
from pose 0.

```{python}
#| label: loop-closure-simulate
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

# Ground truth: 1 m steps around a 10 m square, turning left 90 deg at each
# corner, for one and a quarter laps (51 poses). Pose 40 is back at the start.
steps_per_side = 10
n_poses = 5 * steps_per_side + 1
truth = [np.zeros(3)]
for k in range(n_poses - 1):
    turn = np.pi / 2 if (k + 1) % steps_per_side == 0 else 0.0
    truth.append(compose(truth[-1], np.array([1.0, 0.0, turn])))
truth = np.array(truth)

# Odometry: true relative poses plus white noise plus an unmodeled heading bias.
sigma_odo = np.array([0.05, 0.05, np.deg2rad(1.0)])   # per step [m, m, rad]
heading_bias = np.deg2rad(0.6)                          # per step, not in the model
Omega_odo = np.diag(1.0 / sigma_odo**2)
edges = []
for i in range(n_poses - 1):
    z = relative_pose(truth[i], truth[i + 1]) + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_odo)
    z[2] += heading_bias
    edges.append((i, i + 1, z, Omega_odo))

# One verified loop closure: back at the start, pose 40 is matched to pose 0.
sigma_loop = np.array([0.05, 0.05, np.deg2rad(0.5)])
Omega_loop = np.diag(1.0 / sigma_loop**2)
z_loop = relative_pose(truth[40], truth[0]) + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_loop)
edges.append((40, 0, z_loop, Omega_loop))

# Initial guess: chain the odometry (dead reckoning).
dead_reckoning = [truth[0]]
for i, j, z, _ in edges[: n_poses - 1]:
    dead_reckoning.append(compose(dead_reckoning[-1], z))
dead_reckoning = np.array(dead_reckoning)

gap = np.linalg.norm(dead_reckoning[40, :2] - dead_reckoning[0, :2])
print(f"{n_poses} poses, {len(edges)} edges; dead-reckoned pose 40 is {gap:.2f} m from pose 0")
```

### Linearizing and Solving {#sec-loop-closure-linearizing-solving}

Gauss-Newton linearizes every residual at the current estimate. The update of
each pose is additive in $(x, y, \theta)$, followed by wrapping the heading,
which is a legitimate way to move on $SE(2)$ for small steps. With
$\mathbf{x}_i \leftarrow \mathbf{x}_i + \Delta\mathbf{x}_i$, the residual of
@eq-loop-closure-se2-error-parts changes as
$\mathbf{e}_{ij} + \mathbf{A}_{ij}\Delta\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{B}_{ij}\Delta\mathbf{x}_j$,
with Jacobians

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{A}_{ij} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{ij}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i} &=
\begin{bmatrix}
-\mathbf{C}(\theta_z)^T\mathbf{C}(\theta_i)^T &
\mathbf{C}(\theta_z)^T\,\dfrac{\partial\mathbf{C}(\theta_i)^T}{\partial\theta_i}\,(\mathbf{t}_j - \mathbf{t}_i) \\
\mathbf{0}^T & -1
\end{bmatrix}, \\
\mathbf{B}_{ij} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{e}_{ij}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_j} &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{C}(\theta_z)^T\mathbf{C}(\theta_i)^T & \mathbf{0} \\
\mathbf{0}^T & 1
\end{bmatrix}, \\
\frac{\partial\mathbf{C}(\theta)^T}{\partial\theta} &=
\begin{bmatrix}
-\sin\theta & \cos\theta \\
-\cos\theta & -\sin\theta
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-loop-closure-jacobians}

Substituting the linearized residuals into @eq-loop-closure-pose-graph-cost and
setting the derivative with respect to $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ to zero gives the
normal equations $\mathbf{H}\,\Delta\mathbf{x} = -\mathbf{b}$. Here
$\mathbf{H}$ is the Gauss-Newton information matrix of the whole trajectory,
not a measurement Jacobian (there are only so many letters). Each edge touches
two poses, so it adds four $3 \times 3$ blocks to $\mathbf{H}$ and two
3-vectors to $\mathbf{b}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{H}_{ii} &\mathrel{+}= \mathbf{A}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\mathbf{A}_{ij}, &
\mathbf{H}_{ij} &\mathrel{+}= \mathbf{A}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\mathbf{B}_{ij}, \\
\mathbf{H}_{ji} &\mathrel{+}= \mathbf{B}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\mathbf{A}_{ij}, &
\mathbf{H}_{jj} &\mathrel{+}= \mathbf{B}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\mathbf{B}_{ij}, \\
\mathbf{b}_i &\mathrel{+}= \mathbf{A}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{ij}, &
\mathbf{b}_j &\mathrel{+}= \mathbf{B}_{ij}^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{ij}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-loop-closure-normal-equations}

One more detail before solving. Every measurement is relative, so translating
and rotating the entire trajectory changes no residual. The cost has a
three-dimensional valley of equally good solutions, the **gauge freedom**, and
$\mathbf{H}$ is singular. We fix the gauge by holding pose 0 where it is, which
means deleting its three rows and columns and solving for the remaining poses;
that is the same as a prior on $\mathbf{x}_0$ with infinite information.
Exercise 2 finds the null space this removes.

```{python}
#| label: loop-closure-gauss-newton
def edge_residual_and_jacobians(pose_i, pose_j, z):
    """Residual e = [tau; phi] of E = Z^-1 X_i^-1 X_j, and A = de/dx_i, B = de/dx_j."""
    C_i, C_z = rot2(pose_i[2]), rot2(z[2])
    dt = pose_j[:2] - pose_i[:2]
    e = np.empty(3)
    e[:2] = C_z.T @ (C_i.T @ dt - z[:2])
    e[2] = wrap_angle(pose_j[2] - pose_i[2] - z[2])

    c, s = np.cos(pose_i[2]), np.sin(pose_i[2])
    dCiT_dtheta = np.array([[-s, c], [-c, -s]])
    A = np.zeros((3, 3))
    A[:2, :2] = -C_z.T @ C_i.T
    A[:2, 2] = C_z.T @ dCiT_dtheta @ dt
    A[2, 2] = -1.0
    B = np.zeros((3, 3))
    B[:2, :2] = C_z.T @ C_i.T
    B[2, 2] = 1.0
    return e, A, B


def build_normal_equations(poses, edges, weights=None):
    """Sparse H and b of the linearized pose graph, and the current cost.

    `weights` (one per edge, default 1) scale each information matrix; the
    robust kernels later in the chapter use them.
    """
    n = len(poses)
    rows, cols, vals = [], [], []
    b = np.zeros(3 * n)
    cost = 0.0

    def add_block(i, j, block):
        rows.extend(3 * i + np.repeat(np.arange(3), 3))
        cols.extend(3 * j + np.tile(np.arange(3), 3))
        vals.extend(block.ravel())

    for k, (i, j, z, Omega) in enumerate(edges):
        e, A, B = edge_residual_and_jacobians(poses[i], poses[j], z)
        W = Omega if weights is None else weights[k] * Omega
        add_block(i, i, A.T @ W @ A)
        add_block(i, j, A.T @ W @ B)
        add_block(j, i, B.T @ W @ A)
        add_block(j, j, B.T @ W @ B)
        b[3 * i:3 * i + 3] += A.T @ W @ e
        b[3 * j:3 * j + 3] += B.T @ W @ e
        cost += e @ W @ e
    # Duplicate (row, col) entries are summed when the sparse matrix is built.
    H = sp.csc_matrix((vals, (rows, cols)), shape=(3 * n, 3 * n))
    return H, b, cost


def gauss_newton(initial, edges, weight_fn=None, max_iterations=50, tol=1e-8, verbose=False):
    """Gauss-Newton on the pose graph, holding pose 0 fixed to remove the gauge freedom.

    `weight_fn(poses, edges)`, if given, returns per-edge weights at each
    iteration (iteratively reweighted least squares).
    """
    poses = initial.copy()
    for iteration in range(max_iterations):
        weights = None if weight_fn is None else weight_fn(poses, edges)
        H, b, cost = build_normal_equations(poses, edges, weights)
        dx = np.zeros(3 * len(poses))
        dx[3:] = spla.spsolve(H[3:, 3:], -b[3:])      # pose 0 stays put
        poses = poses + dx.reshape(-1, 3)              # x <- x + dx, then wrap headings
        poses[:, 2] = wrap_angle(poses[:, 2])
        if verbose:
            print(f"iteration {iteration}: cost {cost:9.2f}, max |dx| = {np.abs(dx).max():.1e}")
        if np.abs(dx).max() < tol:
            break
    return poses, H
```

Before trusting the optimizer, check the analytic Jacobians of
@eq-loop-closure-jacobians against central differences. Then run it from the
dead-reckoning guess.

```{python}
#| label: loop-closure-run
# Jacobian check on one edge, at a perturbed estimate so nothing is trivially zero.
i, j, z, _ = edges[17]
pose_i, pose_j = dead_reckoning[i] + [0.1, -0.2, 0.3], dead_reckoning[j]
_, A, B = edge_residual_and_jacobians(pose_i, pose_j, z)
eps = 1e-6
A_num = np.column_stack([(edge_residual_and_jacobians(pose_i + d, pose_j, z)[0]
                          - edge_residual_and_jacobians(pose_i - d, pose_j, z)[0]) / (2 * eps)
                         for d in eps * np.eye(3)])
B_num = np.column_stack([(edge_residual_and_jacobians(pose_i, pose_j + d, z)[0]
                          - edge_residual_and_jacobians(pose_i, pose_j - d, z)[0]) / (2 * eps)
                         for d in eps * np.eye(3)])
print(f"Jacobian check: max |A - A_num| = {np.abs(A - A_num).max():.1e},"
      f" max |B - B_num| = {np.abs(B - B_num).max():.1e}")

optimized, H = gauss_newton(dead_reckoning, edges, verbose=True)


def position_rmse(poses):
    """RMS position error of a trajectory against the simulated truth [m]."""
    return np.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum((poses[:, :2] - truth[:, :2]) ** 2, axis=1)))


print(f"position RMSE: dead reckoning {position_rmse(dead_reckoning):.2f} m,"
      f" pose graph {position_rmse(optimized):.2f} m")
print(f"H is {H.shape[0]} x {H.shape[1]} with {H.nnz} nonzeros"
      f" ({H.nnz / H.shape[0] ** 2:.1%} of the entries)")

# How far is the simple residual [tau; phi] from the exact Log at the solution?
log_gap = max(
    np.abs(se2_log(np.linalg.inv(v2t(z)) @ np.linalg.inv(v2t(optimized[i])) @ v2t(optimized[j]))
           - edge_residual_and_jacobians(optimized[i], optimized[j], z)[0]).max()
    for i, j, z, _ in edges
)
print(f"largest |Log(E) - [tau; phi]| over all edges at the solution: {log_gap:.1e}")
```


Three things in @fig-loop-closure-pose-graph are worth a second look. First,
the correction is not dumped at the end of the loop. The optimizer bends every
odometry edge a little, in proportion to how uncertain the noise model says it
is, so all the poses move, and the error left after optimization is spread
around the loop rather than piled up at pose 40. Second, the poses of the
second lap are pulled along even though no loop closure touches them: they hang
off pose 40 through odometry, so they inherit its correction. Third, the
checks: the analytic Jacobians agree with finite differences, and at the
solution the simple residual $[\boldsymbol{\tau};\ \phi]$ differs from the
exact $\operatorname{Log}$ by an amount far below the noise, as promised.

Panel (c) is the reason graph SLAM scales. Odometry links consecutive poses, so
$\mathbf{H}$ is block-tridiagonal, and each loop closure adds exactly one pair of
off-diagonal blocks. Here about 6% of the entries are nonzero; for a city-scale
graph with $10^5$ poses, a dense $\mathbf{H}$ would have $10^{11}$ entries and
the sparse one a few million. Production solvers factor $\mathbf{H}$ with a
sparse Cholesky decomposition after reordering the variables to limit fill-in.
Dellaert and Kaess's square-root SAM [@dellaert2006] showed that factoring the
sparse square-root information matrix makes full smoothing practical, and
contrasted it with the dense covariance a filter must carry. Compare panel (c)
with @fig-information-fill-in, which is what marginalizing the past poses does
to this same structure.

## Robustness Concerns {#sec-loop-closure-robustness-concerns}

Loop closure failure cases:

- **False negative:** the robot revisits a place but fails to recognize it.
- **False positive:** the robot incorrectly matches two different places.
- **Perceptual aliasing:** different places look geometrically or visually
  similar.
- **Map duplication:** the same physical landmarks are initialized twice.
- **Particle depletion:** the correct revisited-place hypothesis is gone.

The right first response is conservative verification. In navigation, a missed
correction is usually less damaging than a confident false correction. But no
front end is perfect, so the back end needs a second line of defense.

## Robust Kernels for False Loop Closures {#sec-loop-closure-robust-kernels}

Now break the pose graph. On the second pass along the bottom edge the robot
drives past a repetitive stretch (evenly spaced trees, a fence, a corridor of
identical doors), and the front end matches pose 48 with pose 2. They are 6 m
apart. The match says they are the same place, and it says so with exactly the
confidence of the true closure, because the verification step saw a perfectly
good geometric fit: the scenery really does look the same. This is perceptual
aliasing, and front-end verification cannot fully remove it, because each wrong
match is internally consistent. It is inconsistent only with the rest of the
graph.

Least squares has no defense. The squared cost grows quadratically with the
residual, so the most wrong measurement gets the loudest voice. A **robust
kernel** replaces the quadratic with a function $\rho$ that grows more slowly
for large residuals. With $s_k = \mathbf{e}_k^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_k\mathbf{e}_k$
the squared Mahalanobis distance of edge $k$, the cost becomes
$\sum_k \rho(s_k)$. Two classic choices are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\rho_\text{Huber}(s) &=
\begin{cases}
s, & s \le k^2, \\
2k\sqrt{s} - k^2, & s > k^2,
\end{cases} \\
\rho_\text{Cauchy}(s) &= c^2 \ln\left(1 + s / c^2\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-loop-closure-robust-kernels}

The easiest way to minimize a robust cost is **iteratively reweighted least
squares** (IRLS). Setting the gradient of $\sum_k \rho(s_k)$ to zero gives
$\sum_k \rho'(s_k)\,\mathbf{J}_k^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}_k\mathbf{e}_k = \mathbf{0}$,
which is the ordinary weighted least-squares condition with each information
matrix scaled by $w_k = \rho'(s_k)$. So at each Gauss-Newton iteration we
compute the weights from the current residuals and solve the weighted problem:

$$
w_\text{Huber} = \min\left(1, \frac{k}{\sqrt{s}}\right),
\qquad
w_\text{Cauchy} = \frac{1}{1 + s / c^2}.
$$

Huber is quadratic near zero and linear in the Mahalanobis distance beyond $k$:
a bad measurement's pull is capped but never vanishes. Cauchy's influence peaks
and then decays toward zero, so a measurement that is wrong by a lot is all but
ignored. Both use the width $k = c = \sqrt{7.81} = 2.80$, the square root of the
95% chi-square value for three degrees of freedom, the same kind of gate as in
@sec-slam-association-innovation-mahalanobis-distance. Only the loop closures
are robustified; odometry stays quadratic. That is common practice: odometry
edges are trustworthy by construction, and loop closures are the guesses.

```{python}
#| label: loop-closure-robust
# Perceptual aliasing: the front end matches pose 48 with pose 2 (really 6 m
# apart) and reports "same place" with the confidence of a true loop closure.
z_false = rng.normal(0.0, sigma_loop)
edges_false = edges + [(48, 2, z_false, Omega_loop)]
loop_edges = [len(edges) - 1, len(edges)]            # the true and the false closure


def huber_weight(s, k):
    """IRLS weight rho'(s) for the Huber kernel on the Mahalanobis distance sqrt(s)."""
    return min(1.0, k / np.sqrt(s))


def cauchy_weight(s, c):
    """IRLS weight rho'(s) for the Cauchy kernel."""
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + s / c**2)


def robust_weights(kernel, width):
    """Weight function for gauss_newton: robustify the loop closures, trust odometry."""
    def weight_fn(poses, edges):
        w = np.ones(len(edges))
        for k in loop_edges:
            i, j, z, Omega = edges[k]
            e, _, _ = edge_residual_and_jacobians(poses[i], poses[j], z)
            w[k] = kernel(e @ Omega @ e, width)
        return w
    return weight_fn


width = np.sqrt(7.81)        # 95% chi-square gate for 3 degrees of freedom
plain, _ = gauss_newton(dead_reckoning, edges_false)
huber, _ = gauss_newton(dead_reckoning, edges_false, robust_weights(huber_weight, width))
cauchy, _ = gauss_newton(dead_reckoning, edges_false, robust_weights(cauchy_weight, width))

for name, poses in [("dead reckoning", dead_reckoning), ("no false closure", optimized),
                    ("plain least squares", plain), ("Huber", huber), ("Cauchy", cauchy)]:
    print(f"{name:>20}: position RMSE {position_rmse(poses):.2f} m")
for name, kernel, poses in [("Huber", huber_weight, huber), ("Cauchy", cauchy_weight, cauchy)]:
    w = robust_weights(kernel, width)(poses, edges_false)[loop_edges]
    print(f"{name:>6} final weights: true closure {w[0]:.3f}, false closure {w[1]:.1e}")
```

```{python}
                fontsize=8, color="C4")

```

Plain least squares is a disaster. To bring pose 48 onto pose 2 it squeezes the
bottom edge and spreads the damage around the loop, and the result is worse than
not closing the loop at all: compare its error with dead reckoning in the
printout. "A false loop closure can be worse than no loop closure" is not a
figure of speech. Huber recovers most of the map by driving the false closure's
weight down, but because Huber caps the influence rather than removing it, some
distortion remains. Cauchy all but deletes the false closure and returns
essentially the trajectory of the graph that never saw it.

Robust kernels are not magic. The Cauchy cost is not convex, and IRLS finds only
the minimum nearest its starting point. In this example the true closure also
starts with a large residual, since dead reckoning has drifted by a couple of
meters, so at the first iteration both closures look like outliers. It works
because the true closure is much less wrong than the false one, and its weight
recovers as the map straightens. Make the drift larger or the kernel narrower,
and the true closure is rejected too (Exercise 4). That fragility motivates the
literature's more careful answers.

**Switchable constraints** [@sunderhauf2012switchable] give each loop closure a
switch variable between 0 and 1 that the optimizer estimates along with the
poses, with a prior that prefers the switch on; turning a closure off costs
something, but less than keeping a wrong one. **Dynamic covariance scaling**
(DCS) [@agarwal2013dcs] is a closed-form relative of the same idea: it scales
each closure's information by a factor computed from its current residual, which
makes it behave like a redescending robust kernel without extra variables.
**Graduated non-convexity** (GNC) [@yang2020gnc] attacks the initialization
problem directly: it starts from a convex surrogate of the robust cost
(essentially least squares) and morphs it gradually into the nonconvex one, so
the solver never has to find a nonconvex minimum from a bad start, and it
tolerates large fractions of outliers. **Pairwise consistent measurement set
maximization** (PCM) [@mangelson2018pcm] works before optimization: two loop
closures are consistent if composing them with the odometry between them gives a
loop close to the identity, and PCM keeps the largest set of mutually consistent
closures, a maximum-clique problem. It is the loop-closure cousin of joint
compatibility (@sec-slam-association-joint-compatibility).

## Incremental Smoothing in Practice {#sec-loop-closure-incremental-smoothing}

Our optimizer rebuilds and re-solves the whole problem from scratch. That is fine
for 51 poses and for offline mapping, but a robot running for hours adds a pose
every fraction of a second and needs an up-to-date estimate now. A new odometry
edge changes only the newest corner of $\mathbf{H}$, so re-solving the full batch
each time throws away almost all of the previous work. iSAM2 [@kaess2012isam2]
keeps the factorization instead. It represents the factored problem as a
**Bayes tree**, a tree of cliques that is the graphical form of the sparse
square-root information matrix, and when new factors arrive it re-eliminates
only the cliques they touch. It also relinearizes only the variables whose
estimates have moved more than a threshold since they were last linearized. A
new odometry edge then costs almost nothing, while a loop closure touches every
clique on the path from the old pose to the root and costs more, which matches
intuition: a loop closure changes a lot of the past, so it should cost a lot.

iSAM2 is the core of the GTSAM library; g2o and Ceres Solver are the other
common open-source back ends. A typical production architecture runs a filter or
odometry front end at sensor rate and a pose-graph or factor-graph back end in a
separate thread, the division of labor in ORB-SLAM (@sec-visual-nav-orb-slam-as).
@sec-advanced-slam-factor-graphs-smoothing returns to factor graphs with IMU,
GNSS, and camera factors.

## Loop Closure in the Project Report {#sec-loop-closure-project-report}

Project 2 does not ask you to implement pose-graph optimization; the pose graph in
this chapter is for understanding. It asks you to analyze loop closure using your
FastSLAM results (@sec-project2). Questions worth answering in the report:

- Where does the trajectory revisit previously mapped areas, and does it return
  near previously mapped structure where you expect it to?
- Do revisited tree clusters line up in the final map, or does the map show
  duplicate clusters near revisited locations?
- Do candidate old and new landmark sets have compatible geometry (inter-tree
  distances, trunk diameters)?
- How did particle count affect long-term consistency, and did particle
  diversity survive long enough to represent the loop-closing hypothesis?
- How did the resampling threshold affect particle diversity?
- Would a graph-based smoother help? Why?
- What additional front-end information would be needed to add reliable loop
  closures, and how would you protect the back end from a false one?

This is a compare-and-contrast analysis, not another coding assignment.

## Summary {#sec-loop-closure-summary}

Loop closure is essential for long-term consistency, and it is a large topic.
In this module:

1. Place recognition proposes revisits from appearance or geometry, and
   geometric verification turns a candidate into a relative-pose measurement
   with a covariance.
2. Filters can correct the whole map at a loop closure through their
   correlations, but cannot relinearize the past, and particle filters can lose
   the right hypothesis to resampling.
3. A pose graph keeps the past poses, uses the relative-pose residual
   $\operatorname{Log}(\mathbf{Z}_{ij}^{-1}\mathbf{X}_i^{-1}\mathbf{X}_j)$, and
   is solved with sparse Gauss-Newton once the gauge is fixed.
4. A single false loop closure can wreck a least-squares map; robust kernels,
   switchable constraints, GNC, and consistency checks such as PCM are the
   defenses.
5. FastSLAM is the required Project 2 implementation; loop closure is analyzed
   through the behavior of that implementation.

## Exercises {#sec-loop-closure-exercises}

1. **Pose-graph Jacobians.** (a) Derive $\mathbf{A}_{ij}$ and $\mathbf{B}_{ij}$
   in @eq-loop-closure-jacobians from @eq-loop-closure-se2-error-parts.
   (b) Extend the chapter's finite-difference check to 1000 random pose pairs,
   including headings near $\pm\pi$, and report the worst disagreement.
   (c) Show that
   $\mathbf{V}(\phi) = \mathbf{I} + \tfrac{\phi}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + O(\phi^2)$,
   and hence that $\operatorname{Log}(\mathbf{E}_{ij})$ and
   $[\boldsymbol{\tau}_{ij};\ \phi_{ij}]$ differ only at second order in the
   error. Is the printed gap at the solution consistent with that?

2. **Gauge freedom.** Take $\mathbf{H}$ as returned by `gauss_newton` (all
   poses, nothing deleted). (a) Compute its three smallest eigenvalues and show
   that they are zero to numerical precision. (b) Show analytically that the
   null space is spanned by a global $x$ translation, a global $y$ translation,
   and a global rotation whose component for pose $i$ is $[-y_i, x_i, 1]^T$, and
   verify this numerically. (c) Why does the rotation direction depend on the
   current estimate while the translations do not? (d) What happens if you
   anchor only the position of pose 0 and not its heading?

3. **What a loop closure buys.** With pose 0 held fixed, the inverse of the
   reduced $\mathbf{H}$ at the solution approximates the covariance of the other
   poses. Plot the one-sigma position uncertainty,
   $\sqrt{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2}$, along the trajectory with and without the
   loop-closure edge. Where is the uncertainty largest after the loop closes,
   and why is it not at pose 40? What happens to the second-lap poses?

4. **Breaking the robust kernel.** (a) Rerun the false-closure experiment with
   Cauchy widths $c \in \{0.5, 1, 2.8, 10\}$. For which widths is the true
   closure rejected too? For each failure, compare the robust cost at the IRLS
   answer with its value at the clean solution: is the problem the cost function
   or the starting point? (b) Keep $c = 2.8$ and raise the heading bias to
   $1.5^\circ$ per step. Explain the failure from the IRLS weights at the first
   iteration. (c) Implement a simple graduated schedule: start with $c = 100$
   and halve $c$ at each iteration until it reaches 2.8. Does it fix (b)? Does
   it still work at $2^\circ$ per step, and what does real GNC do differently?
   (d) Add five false closures between random pose pairs at least 10 poses
   apart and compare plain least squares, Huber, and Cauchy.

5. **Constellation place recognition for Victoria Park.** Build a tree
   constellation matcher on synthetic data. Scatter 60 trees uniformly over a
   $60 \times 60$ m area with trunk diameters between 0.2 and 0.8 m. The "old
   map" is the trees within 15 m of a point $A$. The "new scan" is the trees
   within 15 m of a point $B$ that is 3 m from $A$, expressed in a frame rotated
   by an unknown angle and shifted by an unknown offset, with 0.1 m position
   noise, 0.05 m diameter noise, 20% missed detections, and two spurious trees.
   (a) Use RANSAC on pairs of trees (two correspondences determine a planar
   transform; prefilter candidate pairs whose inter-tree distance and diameters
   agree) to recover the transform, and report the inlier count. (b) Repeat with
   a "new scan" from a different patch of the forest and compare inlier counts;
   propose an acceptance threshold. (c) Which properties of the real Victoria
   Park detections (@sec-mapping) would make this harder?

6. **The surveyor's compass rule.** A 1D robot starts at $x_0 = 0$ (known) and
   makes $N$ odometry steps, $x_k = x_{k-1} + u_k + w_k$ with
   $w_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, q)$, then measures a loop closure
   $z = x_N + v$ with $v \sim \mathcal{N}(0, r)$. (a) Show that the
   least-squares (smoothed) estimate is
   $\hat{x}_k = x_k^\text{DR} + \frac{kq}{Nq + r}\left(z - x_N^\text{DR}\right)$,
   where $x_k^\text{DR}$ is dead reckoning: the misclosure is distributed in
   proportion to the number of steps, which is distance traveled when the steps
   are equal. Land surveyors have adjusted traverses this way since Nathaniel
   Bowditch proposed the "compass rule" in the early 1800s, the same Bowditch
   whose *American Practical Navigator* is still carried on US ships
   [@bowditch2019]. (b) Show that the posterior variance is
   $\sigma_k^2 = kq - (kq)^2 / (Nq + r)$ and find where it peaks when $r \to 0$.
   (c) Because $x_0$ is known, $z$ acts here like an absolute fix. Show that a
   Kalman filter carrying only the current pose gets $\hat{x}_N$ exactly right
   but leaves $\hat{x}_k$, $k < N$, at dead reckoning, and name the algorithm
   from @sec-kf-smoothing that recovers the rest. Why would the filter's
   $\hat{x}_N$ no longer match the smoother's for a planar robot with an
   uncertain heading?
